\title{A nuclear-spin quantum reservoir computer on real-world forecasting:\\
pre-registered confirmation of non-inferiority, not superiority,\\
to tuned classical models}

\author{[Author list to confirm]}

% Sources for the abstract: QRC_Design_Evidence.md (Confirmation 1, Confirmation 2, F3),
% QRC_Design_Concepts.md sections 11-12 outcomes (Confirmation 3, drift test), qrc_diag_lagos.json
% (f3_pooled_9), QRC_RealWorld_Benchmark.md (tally), qrc_paired_tests.md (synthetic ratios).
\begin{abstract}
Claims for quantum reservoir computing (QRC) rest mostly on synthetic benchmarks and
on comparisons with weakly tuned classical models. We instead evaluate a simulated
nine-spin $^{13}$C crotonic-acid nuclear-magnetic-resonance (NMR) reservoir---exact
Lindblad dynamics, the standard 653-bin free-induction-decay (FID) spectral readout
($D=653$), linear ridge readout---on real-world forecasting, against a tuned echo-state
network (ESN), a tuned LSTM and a tuned linear autoregressive (AR) model. Every
dataset is split chronologically, every choice is made on validation data, and
every design change is frozen and pre-registered in a version-controlled commit
before it is confirmed on cities whose data had never been downloaded. On nine
development datasets the best QRC variant (a learned input encoding) was never
significantly better than the tuned ESN and was significantly worse on five. A memory analysis traced the long-horizon gap to
input overwrite, and a single physical parameter---an encoding gain $g$ that scales the
input pulse angle, frozen at $g=0.35$ on validation data---improved the pooled test
$R^2$ over the standard encoding ($g=1$) in all six cities where it was tested, a
pooled-$R^2$ gain of $+0.015$ to $+0.079$. Five further pre-registered changes (bounded features, step time
and compact readout, a learned encoding on top of the gain, a kernel readout, and
$^{13}$C or population readouts) were not adopted or failed confirmation; all are
reported. The encoding of the closest experimental work scores below the frozen gain. In the second confirmation the frozen
design is non-inferior to the tuned ESN, LSTM and linear AR in 3/3 cities (margin
$0.02$ in $R^2$, set after the first confirmation and disclosed). Over all nine
untouched cities it is within the margin of the tuned ESN in 7/9, of the LSTM in 8/9
and of linear AR in 9/9, but never better than the ESN, which is significantly ahead
in 6/9 (mean $\Delta R^2=-0.011$; worst in Lagos, $-0.049$, where slow temperature
anomalies demand long memory). The QRC fails under input distribution shift; a
pre-registered test on two untouched, shifted series confirms that classical level
handling (last-value re-centring plus raw input lags) removes most of the failure, but
it gives the QRC no edge over the tuned classical models. On synthetic tasks a
gradient-trained encoding improves the reservoir through its cross-step memory, yet a
tuned ESN is one to three orders of magnitude better. We claim non-inferiority to tuned
classical models on most untouched real-world data, and no quantum advantage.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

% ======================================================================
\section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}
Reservoir computing (RC) trains only a linear readout on the state of a fixed
nonlinear dynamical system, avoiding the cost and instability of training a recurrent
core~\cite{Jaeger2001,Maass2002,Lukosevicius2009,Tanaka2019}. Quantum reservoir
computing (QRC) replaces the classical reservoir with a quantum system whose large
state space and intrinsic nonlinearity are conjectured to provide a rich temporal
kernel at low training cost~\cite{Fujii2017,Nakajima2019,Mujal2021}. Nuclear-spin
ensembles are an attractive QRC substrate: many coupled qubits, well-characterized
Hamiltonians, decades of control technology, and a native, ensemble-averaged
time-multiplexed observable---the free-induction decay
(FID)~\cite{Negoro2018,Hou2026,VandersypenChuang2005}.

Two features of the QRC literature make its practical value hard to judge. First,
most evidence comes from synthetic benchmarks (NARMA, Mackey--Glass, memory
capacity), where a well-tuned classical reservoir is a demanding reference. Second,
the classical baseline is often weakly tuned. Our own synthetic results illustrate
both points: on NARMA and Mackey--Glass a gradient-trained QRC encoding beats a tuned
LSTM on two of three tasks, but a fully tuned ESN is one to three orders of magnitude
better on all three (Sec.~\ref{sec:mechanism}). We therefore make real-world
forecasting the primary test, and design the study so that its conclusion cannot be
produced by selection on the test data.

The study has three stages. (i) A \emph{development benchmark} on nine real-world
datasets (daily weather, hourly air quality and transformer load, a chaotic laser),
in which the standard QRC is compared with a tuned ESN, LSTM and linear AR model
(Sec.~\ref{sec:bench}). (ii) Six \emph{design steps}, each pre-registered in a
commit before it was run, developed on validation periods only and adopted only if it
cleared a fixed threshold (Sec.~\ref{sec:design}). (iii) Three \emph{pre-registered
confirmations} on nine cities, and a pre-registered \emph{drift test} on two shifted
non-weather series, whose data were downloaded only after the rules and success
criteria were committed (Secs.~\ref{sec:confirm} and \ref{sec:drift}). A short
section uses synthetic tasks, where ablations are cheap, to ask which parts of the
reservoir carry the computation (Sec.~\ref{sec:mechanism}).

Our contributions are: (1) a leakage-controlled, pre-registered real-world
forecasting protocol for a physical QRC, with all failures reported; (2) the finding
that the long-horizon gap of an NMR reservoir is largely input overwrite, removable by
one physical parameter (the encoding gain), confirmed out of sample in six untouched
cities; (3) pre-registered evidence on nine untouched cities that the final design is
mostly non-inferior to---but never better than---tuned classical models, with the
remaining gap located in long memory; (4) a pre-registered drift test showing
that the QRC's failure under input shift is fixed by classical level handling, not by
the reservoir; and (5) a physics-informed readout derived from the Hamiltonian, which
projects the FID onto its analytic $J$-multiplet lines. It matches the 653-bin readout
with about $3\times$ fewer features and is differentiable
(Sec.~\ref{sec:mech-readout}).

\section{The physical reservoir and its readout}\label{sec:model}

on the output side, together with the pre-registered changes that were tested and not

\subsection{Physical platform}
We consider liquid-state NMR of an isotopically labeled molecule in a strong static
field $B_0\hat z$. The sample is a macroscopic ensemble ($\sim\!10^{18}$ molecules),
so every observable is an ensemble average: the induced FID is a classical voltage
proportional to the expectation value $\langle\hat O\rangle=\Tr(\hat O\rho)$, obtained
without single-shot projection noise. This suits reservoir computing, where the
readout is precisely a set of such expectation values. The reservoir for all
real-world results is the nine-spin $^{13}$C-labeled crotonic-acid molecule (four
carbons, five protons, the three methyl protons magnetically
equivalent)~\cite{Hou2026} (Table~\ref{tab:crotonic}). The mechanism study
(Sec.~\ref{sec:mechanism}) additionally uses a seven-spin $^{13}$C molecule (dccb7)
and an abstract six-spin Ising reservoir.

\subsection{Rotating-frame Hamiltonian}
In the rotating frame of each spin's Larmor frequency and under the weak-coupling
(secular) approximation valid when $|\nu_i-\nu_j|\gg|J_{ij}|$, the internal
Hamiltonian reduces to a diagonal Ising form,
\begin{equation}
  \frac{H}{h} = \sum_i \nu_i\, I_z^{(i)}
            \;+\; \sum_{i<j} J_{ij}\, I_z^{(i)} I_z^{(j)},
  \qquad I_z=\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma_z,
  \label{eq:H}
\end{equation}
with chemical-shift offsets $\nu_i$ (Hz) and scalar $J$-couplings $J_{ij}$ (Hz);
angular frequencies carry the usual factor $2\pi$. All terms commute, so
Eq.~\eqref{eq:H} is diagonal in the computational basis $\{\ket{z}\}$,
$z\in\{\pm1\}^n$, with eigenvalues
\begin{equation}
  E(z)/h = \tfrac12\sum_i \nu_i z_i + \tfrac14\sum_{i<j} J_{ij} z_i z_j .
  \label{eq:E}
\end{equation}
Entanglement is generated purely by the $ZZ$ evolution acting on the transverse
coherences that the input and readout pulses create; the diagonal structure makes the
FID line structure analytic (Sec.~\ref{sec:mech-readout}).

\subsection{Dissipation}
Relaxation is modeled by a Lindblad master equation,
\begin{equation}
  \dot\rho = -\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,\rho]
     + \sum_i\!\Big(\mathcal D[\hat L_i^{T_1}]\rho + \mathcal D[\hat L_i^{T_2}]\rho\Big),
  \quad \mathcal D[\hat L]\rho=\hat L\rho\hat L^\dagger-\tfrac12\{\hat L^\dagger\hat L,\rho\},
  \label{eq:lindblad}
\end{equation}
with longitudinal (amplitude-damping) and pure-dephasing jump operators
\begin{equation}
  \hat L_i^{T_1}=\sqrt{1/T_{1,i}}\,\sigma_-^{(i)},\qquad
  \hat L_i^{T_2}=\sqrt{\gamma_{\phi,i}/2}\,\sigma_z^{(i)},\quad
  \gamma_{\phi,i}=\frac{1}{T_{2,i}}-\frac{1}{2T_{1,i}} ,
  \label{eq:jumps}
\end{equation}
the physical (Bloch--Redfield-consistent) dephasing rate. We use measured $T_1$ and
$T_2^\ast$ for the crotonic system (Table~\ref{tab:crotonic}).

\subsection{Initial state}
At room temperature and NMR fields the spins are in the high-temperature limit; the
equilibrium density matrix is, to leading order,
$\rho_0\propto \mathbb{1}+\epsilon\sum_i I_z^{(i)}$. We take the product form
$\rho_0=\bigotimes_i(\mathbb 1+\epsilon\sigma_z^{(i)})/2$ with $\epsilon=0.05$. Because
Eqs.~\eqref{eq:lindblad}--\eqref{eq:jumps} are linear in $\rho$, the value of
$\epsilon$ scales the overall signal amplitude but not the qualitative dynamics.

\subsection{Input encoding and the encoding gain}\label{sec:encoding}
A scalar input $s\in[0,1]$ is written into the reservoir as a resonant
radio-frequency rotation $R_x(\theta)=\exp\!\big(-i\,\theta\textstyle\sum_{i} I_x^{(i)}\big)$
on the addressed spins. The standard encoding is $\theta(s)=\arcsin\sqrt{s}$, chosen so
that a uniform input distribution maps to a uniform distribution of state
overlaps~\cite{Hou2026}. We introduce an \emph{encoding gain} $g\in(0,1]$,
\begin{equation}
  \theta(s) = g\,\arcsin\sqrt{s},
  \label{eq:gain}
\end{equation}
so that $g=1$ is the standard encoding. A smaller $g$ rotates the stored state less
on every step (less overwrite of the population memory) at the price of weaker input
injection---the same trade-off that an ESN's input scale controls. For two-variable
inputs (e.g.\ temperature and humidity) the first variable drives the protons and the
second the carbons; a single-variable input drives every spin.
% Source: backend/scripts/qrc_realworld_bench.py docstring (var0 -> protons, var1 -> carbons).

\subsection{Free evolution, time multiplexing, and the standard FID readout}\label{sec:readout}
Each input step consists of (i) the encoding pulse $\rho\!\to\!U\rho U^\dagger$ and
(ii) free evolution under Eq.~\eqref{eq:lindblad} for a fixed time
$\tau=\SI{30}{ms}$ (SOP standard). The readout is the proton FID, the transverse
magnetization
\begin{equation}
  M^{+}(t)=\sum_{k\in\mathrm{readout}} \big\langle\sigma_x^{(k)}\big\rangle(t)
            + i\big\langle\sigma_y^{(k)}\big\rangle(t),
  \label{eq:fid}
\end{equation}
sampled densely in time; the dense sampling is itself the time multiplexing that
enlarges the feature space~\cite{Nakajima2019}. In the simulation the FID is read
from a copy of the state after each step. The feature vector of a step is the
magnitude of the FFT of the FID at the 653 largest-magnitude bins (fixed once), the
readout of Ref.~\cite{Hou2026}; we call it the \emph{653-bin FID readout}, $D=653$.
\textbf{All real-world results in this paper use this readout.} A linear ridge
readout $W=(X^\top X+\alpha I)^{-1}X^\top y$ maps the features to every forecast
target; whether the features are standardized and the penalty $\alpha$ are chosen on
validation data (Sec.~\ref{sec:protocol}).

\subsection{Physics-informed line readout}\label{sec:mech-readout}
% Source: SOP section 3.2 (QRC_STANDARD_PROCEDURES.md); line counts from
% backend/app/qrc/spectral_lines.py physics_informed_lines (crotonic-9 protons 1280 / 1.57 Hz / 100;
% dccb7 all seven 448 / 0.60 Hz / 172, recomputed 2026-10-25); 6-spin rows as the earlier manuscript.
The 653-bin readout selects FFT bins by magnitude. We also derive the readout from the
Hamiltonian. Because $H$ in Eq.~\eqref{eq:H} is diagonal, the FID
Eq.~\eqref{eq:fid} is a sum over \emph{single-quantum} transitions: flipping readout
spin $k$ against a fixed configuration $z\in\{\pm1\}^{n-1}$ of the other spins
oscillates, from Eq.~\eqref{eq:E}, at
\begin{equation}
  f_k(z) = \nu_k + \tfrac12\!\sum_{j\neq k} J_{kj}\,z_j .
  \label{eq:lines}
\end{equation}
Each resonance is split into a $2^{n-1}$-line $J$-multiplet, and every peak of the
653-bin readout is one of these lines or an FFT skirt of one. The encoding sets only
the line amplitudes; the frequencies are fixed by $H$. Merging lines closer than the
decoherence linewidth $\Delta f=1/(\pi T_2)$ leaves $D_{\mathrm{eff}}$ resolvable
centres (Table~\ref{tab:deff}), which are read by a fixed direct-DFT projection
\begin{equation}
  X_k = \sum_{v=0}^{V-1} M^{+}(t_v)\, e^{\,i 2\pi f_k t_v}
      = \big(M^{+}\Phi\big)_k,\qquad \Phi_{v,k}=e^{\,i2\pi f_k t_v},
  \label{eq:proj}
\end{equation}
over $V$ FID samples, keeping real and imaginary parts: $D=2D_{\mathrm{eff}}$ real
features. This \emph{line readout} has three properties. It counts the reservoir's
actual output dimension instead of choosing it. It is a single matrix product, so it
can be back-propagated through, which the learned encoding of regime B requires
(Sec.~\ref{sec:regimes}). And it keeps the phase that $|$FFT$|$ discards. On real data
at $g=0.35$, crotonic-9's 100 proton lines ($D=200$) reach a mean development
validation $R^2$ of 0.7021 against 0.7059 for the 653 bins, with about $3\times$ fewer
features (Table~\ref{tab:c5c7}). It was not adopted because the rule required a gain,
but it is the readout of every mechanism result (Sec.~\ref{sec:mechanism}).

\subsection{Numerical methods}
We vectorize the density matrix, $\rho\!\to\!\vec\rho\in\mathbb{C}^{d^2}$ ($d=2^n$), and
write Eq.~\eqref{eq:lindblad} as $\dot{\vec\rho}=\mathcal L\vec\rho$. Because $H$ is
diagonal and the dissipators preserve coherence order, $\exp(\tau\mathcal L)$ is exact
and block-diagonal in coherence patterns; for $n\ge7$ we use this exact block
propagator, which makes multi-decade daily series tractable for nine spins. For small systems ($d^2\le 8192$) we precompute the dense node
propagator, which is also differentiable (Sec.~\ref{sec:mechanism}).

\subsection{Two training regimes}\label{sec:regimes}
We distinguish, and label on every result, two regimes. In \textbf{regime A} (standard
QRC) the reservoir and the encoding are fixed and only the linear readout is
trained by one closed-form ridge solve. In \textbf{regime B} (learned encoding) the
same ridge readout is used, but the input encoding is additionally trained by
gradient descent through the differentiable reservoir. The final real-world design is
regime A: the encoding gain $g$ is a fixed hyperparameter, frozen on validation data,
not a trained weight.

\section{Benchmark protocol}\label{sec:protocol}
% Sources: QRC_RealWorld_Benchmark.md (protocol), QRC_Design_Concepts.md sections 3, 6-10,
% backend/scripts/qrc_realworld_bench.py (dataset splits).

\subsection{Datasets and chronological splits}
Every dataset is split chronologically into train / validation / test blocks, fixed
before any result. Normalization (min--max) uses pre-test data only. The nine
\emph{development} datasets are: daily temperature and relative humidity of Delhi from
a Kaggle station record (the task of Ref.~\cite{Hou2026}; 300 training days, 500 test
days); Open-Meteo ERA5 reanalysis daily temperature and humidity, 1970--2025, for Delhi,
Mumbai, Bangkok, Beijing and Berlin (train 1971--1999, validation 2000--2004, test 2005
to the end of the record, 7625 test days); the hourly Beijing PM2.5 station record
(temperature and dew point; train 2010--2012, validation 2013, test 2014); the ETTh1
transformer record (inputs oil temperature and load, target oil temperature, standard
12/4/4-month split); and the Santa Fe laser A chaotic series. Weather targets are each
variable at horizons $h=1,5,10,15,20,30,45$~days (14 targets); the other datasets use
their own horizon sets. % TODO add dataset citations (ERA5/Open-Meteo, ETDataset, UCI PRSA, Santa Fe) -- no bib keys yet.
The nine \emph{confirmation} datasets are further ERA5 cities with exactly the ERA5
protocol: Chennai, Cairo and Moscow (Confirmation 1), Sydney, S\~{a}o Paulo and
Toronto (Confirmation 2), and Lagos, Mexico City and Stockholm (Confirmation 3), chosen
for climatic diversity; ETTh2 serves as the untouched distribution-shift test of design
step~2. The \emph{drift test} (Sec.~\ref{sec:drift}) uses two standard long-term
forecasting series: daily exchange rates 1990--2016 (target the first currency, second
input the second; horizons 1, 5, 10, 20 days) and hourly electricity consumption
2012--2014 (target the last of 321 clients, second input the mean over all clients;
horizons 1, 6, 12, 24, 48~h), each split chronologically 70/10/20\%.

\subsection{Models and validation-only selection}
\emph{QRC}: the crotonic-9 reservoir of Sec.~\ref{sec:model}, 653-bin FID readout
($D=653$), ridge readout with $\alpha$ and the standardization flag chosen on
validation, refit on train+validation, test read once. \emph{Tuned ESN}: leaky ESN, grid
over size ($\le1000$) $\times$ spectral radius $\times$ leak $\times$ input scale
(three reservoir seeds), selected on validation; a \emph{size-matched} ESN restricts
the size to $\le653$, the QRC's feature count. \emph{Tuned LSTM}~\cite{Hochreiter1997}:
hidden size $\times$ layers $\times$ learning rate, three initializations, early
stopping on validation $R^2$, the selected configuration retrained on train+validation
for the selected epoch count. \emph{Tuned linear AR}: ridge regression on lagged
inputs, lags and penalty chosen on validation. No model sees the test block before its
configuration is fixed.

\subsection{Metric and significance}
The metric is the pooled test $R^2$, the mean over all forecast targets
(variables $\times$ horizons); higher is better. Short horizons are $h\le10$ days and
long horizons $h\ge30$ days. Uncertainty is a 95\% moving-block bootstrap over test
time (2000 resamples; 30-day blocks in the confirmations), paired on the same test
days, applied to the \emph{difference} in pooled $R^2$ between two models. A
difference is called significant when its CI excludes 0. Replicate s.d.\ (encoder,
reservoir or initialization seeds) is reported where a model has replicates; the
fixed-encoding QRC is deterministic.

\subsection{Development, freezing, and pre-registration}
The test blocks of the nine development datasets were scored once in the development
benchmark (Sec.~\ref{sec:bench}); from then on they are treated as \emph{seen}. All
subsequent design work (Sec.~\ref{sec:design}) used development \emph{validation}
periods only. Each design step was written as a pre-registration---the search space,
a freeze rule with a numerical adoption threshold, and the success criteria of its
confirmation---and committed to the project repository before it was run. Each
confirmation's data were downloaded only after its pre-registration was committed.
Table~\ref{tab:prereg} lists the commits and outcomes; all outcomes, including
failures, are reported.

\section{Development benchmark}\label{sec:bench}

($g=1$), with the fixed encoding (``arcsin'', regime A) and with a per-spin encoding
correction trained on a training-period slice (``learned'', regime B, three encoder

ESN it was never significantly better, comparable on 4 and significantly worse on 5;

\paragraph*{Why the QRC loses where it loses.}
% Source: QRC_RealWorld_Factors.md (post-hoc, correlational; qrc_realworld_factors.json,
% qrc_realworld_memory_function.json).
A post-hoc factor analysis over 101 forecast targets (ETTh1 excluded) identified
forecast horizon as the main factor against the ESN: the QRC$-$ESN difference falls
with horizon (Spearman $-0.47$), from $-0.0001$ at short horizons to $-0.041$ at long
horizons. The memory function (test $R^2$ of reconstructing the input $L$ steps back,
ERA5 Delhi) makes this direct: the QRC reaches 0.92 / 0.77 / 0.53 at lags 10 / 30 / 90
days, the tuned ESN 0.97 / 0.94 / 0.88. The QRC's memory outlasts its coherence time
(7--11 steps), so population memory already reaches the readout; the likely limiter is
that every input pulse, up to $\pi/2$ per spin, partly overwrites the stored
populations. In ESN language, the standard QRC runs at a large, fixed input scale.
Two further factors: the QRC beats the LSTM only where the LSTM is data- or
signal-starved, and on ETTh1 the test period shifts regime (inputs 1.31 s.d.\ from
the training mean) so that the unbounded FFT features leave their training range (up to
16--29 s.d.), whereas the ESN's bounded states degrade gracefully. A tuned linear AR
model is within 0.01--0.04 $R^2$ of the best nonlinear model on most weather targets,
and is the best model on ETTh1. These observations motivated the design concepts of
Sec.~\ref{sec:design}; because they were made on seen test data, nothing in them is
claimed until confirmed on untouched data.

% ======================================================================
\section{Design steps (validation data only)}\label{sec:design}
% Source: QRC_Design_Evidence.md steps 1-4 (generated from qrc_design_*.json);
% QRC_Design_Concepts.md sections 6-9.
Each step below was pre-registered (Table~\ref{tab:prereg}) and developed on the
validation periods of the eight counted development datasets (Kaggle Delhi, with only
300 training days and a 60-day inner split, is reported separately as a small-data
check). No test block is used in any step except the untouched ETTh2 confirmation of
step~2 and a labelled post-hoc check of step~5 on the already-seen ETT test sets.

\subsection{Step 1: encoding gain}\label{sec:step1}
We swept $g\in\{0.1,0.2,0.35,0.5,0.75,1\}$ in Eq.~\eqref{eq:gain} (regime A, no
training). Lowering $g$ raised the memory function at a mid lag on all eight datasets
(H1 supported, 8/8) and improved long-horizon validation $R^2$ by at least half the
benchmark gap ($\ge0.0205$) without losing short horizons on six of eight (H2 met,
6/8) (Table~\ref{tab:gain}). Because ``best $g$'' is chosen and scored on the same
validation period, the per-dataset optimum is optimistic; the robust finding is the
trend. The frozen rule is a single fixed gain, $g=0.35$: it has the best mean rank over
the eight datasets (2.12 of 6 gains), the best mean long-horizon validation $R^2$
(0.618), ties the best mean pooled validation $R^2$ (0.700), and beats $g=1$ on all
eight. At $g=0.1$ the readout becomes ill-conditioned on small data (Kaggle Delhi
validation $R^2$ down to $-6.3$), so the best gain is data-regime dependent.
Figure~\ref{fig:memory} shows the mechanism: lowering $g$ from 1 to 0.35 lifts the
memory of the input 90 days back from 0.62 to 0.79, but no gain reaches the tuned ESN
(0.88); below $g=0.35$ nothing more is gained.

\subsection{Step 2: bounded readout features (not supported)}
To address the ETTh1 drift failure, three bounded transforms of the 653 features
(clipped $z$-score, $\tanh(z/3)$, training-set rank), fitted on training data, were
compared on development validation at $g=0.35$; $\tanh(z/3)$ was frozen (mean 0.7067
vs raw 0.7061) before the untouched ETTh2 series was downloaded. On ETTh2 the
pre-registered criterion failed: pooled test $R^2$ was $+0.2914$ with the transform
vs $+0.3632$ raw (difference $-0.0717$, CI $[-0.1880,+0.0320]$), against
$+0.7911$ (tuned ESN), $+0.7467$ (tuned LSTM) and $+0.8113$ (linear AR). The drift
failure replicates out of sample for the standard QRC ($g=1$: $R^2=-0.1506$). The cause
is extrapolation, not feature size: under drift the inputs leave the training range,
where the QRC's strongly nonlinear feature map gives the linear readout no reliable
relation. The frozen gain lifts the QRC from $-0.15$ to $+0.36$ on ETTh2 (not
pre-registered for ETTh2), still about 0.4 below the classical models. This is a
documented limitation.

\subsection{Step 3: step time and compact readout (not adopted)}
At $g=0.35$ we scored $\tau\in\{15,30,60,100\}$~ms $\times$ six readouts (653, 200 and
100 top bins; PCA to 128 and 64; the physics-informed line projection of
Sec.~\ref{sec:mech-readout}) on development validation (Table~\ref{tab:c5c7}). The
current design ($\tau=\SI{30}{ms}$, 653 bins, mean 0.7059) was the best of all 24
combinations, so nothing was adopted and no confirmation was run. The optimum in
$\tau$ is flat once the gain is set; the line projection is near-equal (0.7021) with
${\sim}3\times$ fewer features, and on the small Kaggle Delhi set compact readouts
help slightly (0.590 vs 0.582 at \SI{30}{ms}).

\subsection{Step 4: learned encoding on top of the gain (not adopted)}\label{sec:step4}
We trained a per-spin correction $\theta=0.35\arcsin\sqrt{s}+0.5\tanh(\mathrm{MLP}(s))$,
zero-initialized so that training starts at the current design, with the recipe of the
development benchmark (training-period slice only, 30 Adam steps, seeds 0--2;
regime B, 653-bin readout). Its seed-mean validation $R^2$ was 0.7038 vs 0.7059 for the
fixed gain ($\Delta=-0.0021$, threshold $+0.005$; better on 4 of 8), so it was not
adopted. The fixed $g=0.35$ also beats the published learned encoding at $g=1$ on 6 of
8 datasets (mean 0.7059 vs 0.6927). On real data, therefore, the learned-encoding gain
of the development benchmark is largely explained by reduced input overwrite, and the
two improvements are not complementary: once $g$ is reduced, the learned correction
mostly fits the training slice without transferring to validation.

\subsection{Step 5: readout-side variants (kernel adopted, then withdrawn)}\label{sec:step5}
% Source: QRC_Design_Concepts.md section 11 + "Step 5 outcome"; qrc_design_r_{dev_*,frozen,posthoc_*}.json.
Five readout-side variants were added on top of the 653 features and given identically
to the tuned ESN (validation-selected hyperparameters): last-value re-centring
(``delta''), raw input lags (``lags'', and both together, ``level handling''), a ridge
fit to the residual of the tuned linear AR, delay-embedded feature principal
components (classical memory, labelled as such), and a random-Fourier-feature kernel
readout (2000 features). By the pre-registered rule the kernel readout was adopted
(mean development validation $R^2$ 0.7115 vs 0.7061; worse on 2/8), but the whole gain
came from Santa Fe ($+0.059$); without it the change was $-0.002$. It then failed its
confirmation (Sec.~\ref{sec:conf3}) and is withdrawn. A post-hoc check on the seen ETT
test sets, labelled as such, showed the kernel readout collapsing under drift and
level handling helping (ETTh2 $+0.36\to+0.74$, ETTh1 $-0.21\to+0.23$); that
observation is what the drift test of Sec.~\ref{sec:drift} confirms on untouched data.

\subsection{Step 6: published encoding and population readouts (not adopted)}\label{sec:step6}
% Source: QRC_Design_Concepts.md section 13 + "Step 6 outcome"; qrc_design_p_frozen.json, qrc_design_p{A,B}_dev_*.json.
Two physical changes remained after step 5. (A) The encoding of the closest experimental
work, $\theta=\arcsin s$~\cite{Hou2026}, as a positioning control. (B) Reading the
long-lived $^{13}$C spins ($T_1$ up to \SI{27.5}{s}) as well as the protons: a $^{13}$C
FID (653 bins), the nine single-spin $\langle\sigma_z\rangle$, or all 512
computational-basis populations (idealised; population tomography on hardware), each
concatenated with the proton readout ($D=662$--$1306$). The adoption rule was that of
step 5, plus a guard learned there: the gain must survive dropping the single
most-improved dataset. Nothing was adopted (Table~\ref{tab:step6}). The published
encoding scored 0.6903 against 0.7060 for $g=0.35$ (worse on 5/8; better than
$\arcsin\sqrt{s}$ at $g=1$, 0.6798, since $\arcsin s\le\arcsin\sqrt{s}$ also rotates
less). The best readout, proton $\oplus$ $^{13}$C FID, gained $+0.0023$, almost all of
it on Santa Fe, and no channel changed the long-lag memory on any weather city
(Delhi, lag 90: 0.79 for every channel). The memory gap is therefore not a readout
limit: the proton $J$-multiplets already resolve the carbon configurations, and since
$H$ is diagonal the populations change only through the input pulses and $T_1$.
Memory is set by how each pulse overwrites the stored state, which no readout can
undo.

\paragraph*{Final design.} Steps 1--6 leave the final design: crotonic-9, fixed gain
$g=0.35$ (no learned correction), $\tau=\SI{30}{ms}$, 653-bin FID readout ($D=653$),
ridge readout. It is regime A: no gradient enters the quantum dynamics. Where inputs
can drift, level handling is added to the readout as classical features
(Sec.~\ref{sec:drift}).

% ======================================================================
\section{Pre-registered confirmations on untouched cities}\label{sec:confirm}
% Sources: QRC_Design_Evidence.md (Confirmation 1, Confirmation 2, F3);
% absolute R^2 per model from docs/QRC/data/qrc_confirm1_<city>.json and
% qrc_confirm2_<city>.json ("groups.<model>.pooled"); QRC_Design_Concepts.md sections 6, 10.

\subsection{Confirmation 1: the gain rule}
Pre-registered in commit \texttt{29152bf} before the data were downloaded, Confirmation
1 tested the frozen gain on Chennai, Cairo and Moscow (test 2005--2025, 7625 days, read
once). S1 passed in 3/3 cities and S2 passed: the mean long-horizon gain was $+0.0757$
(threshold $+0.0205$) and the mean short-horizon gain $+0.0185$ (no loss)
(Tables~\ref{tab:confirmR2} and \ref{tab:confirmDelta}). A secondary rule---re-selecting
$g$ on each city's own validation period---picked $g=0.5$ in Chennai and Cairo and was
worse there than the fixed rule (Cairo: $+0.0026$, CI $[-0.0041,+0.0102]$ over $g=1$): a
single frozen gain generalized better than per-city re-tuning. Descriptively, the gain
closed most of the gap to the tuned ESN without overtaking it (comparable in Cairo,
ESN significantly better in Chennai and Moscow).

\subsection{Confirmation 2: the final design}
After steps 2--4 left the design unchanged, Confirmation 2 (commit \texttt{7965cde},
before the data were downloaded) tested the final design on Sydney, S\~{a}o Paulo and
Toronto with the same protocol and two pre-registered criteria: F1, a replication of
the gain effect ($\Delta(g{=}0.35-g{=}1)>0$ with CI excluding 0 in $\ge2/3$ cities); and
F2, non-inferiority with margin $\delta=0.02$ in pooled $R^2$, separately for each
baseline $b\in\{$tuned ESN, tuned LSTM, linear AR$\}$: the CI lower bound of
$\Delta(\mathrm{final}-b)$ must exceed $-0.02$ in $\ge2/3$ cities. No superiority over
the ESN would be claimed unless a CI lay wholly above 0.

\emph{Disclosure.} The margin $\delta=0.02$ was set with knowledge of the Confirmation 1
results, in which the final design's CI lower bounds against the tuned ESN were
$-0.0220$, $-0.0054$ and $-0.0160$; the Confirmation 2 data were untouched when it was
set. Applied retrospectively to Confirmation 1, the same margin would pass against the
ESN in 2/3 cities (Chennai fails at $-0.0220$), against the LSTM in 2/3 (Moscow fails
at $-0.0213$) and against linear AR in 3/3.
% Retrospective check computed from the Confirmation 1 S3 CIs in QRC_Design_Evidence.md.

\emph{Outcome.} F1 passed in 3/3 cities (gains $+0.0238$, $+0.0513$, $+0.0257$; long-horizon
gains $+0.0465$ to $+0.1035$). F2 passed for every baseline in 3/3 cities. Against the
tuned baselines the final design is within 0.009 $R^2$ of the best model in every city:
the tuned ESN remains significantly better in Sydney ($-0.0089$) and Toronto
($-0.0046$) and is tied in S\~{a}o Paulo; the tuned LSTM is significantly better only in
Sydney ($-0.0048$); the QRC is significantly better than linear AR in Sydney and S\~{a}o
Paulo.

\subsection{Confirmation 3: the kernel readout (not confirmed)}\label{sec:conf3}
% Source: qrc_confirm3_{lagos,mexicocity,stockholm}.json; QRC_Design_Concepts.md "Confirmation 3 outcome";
% base-design F3 CIs vs LSTM / AR: qrc_diag_lagos.json f3_per_city (same bootstrap as qrc_design_r.py).
Confirmation 3 (commit \texttt{a7cb3e6}, before the data were downloaded) tested the
step-5 kernel readout on Lagos, Mexico City and Stockholm. G1 required it to beat the
plain ridge readout (CI excluding 0) in $\ge2/3$ cities; it was significantly
\emph{worse} in all three ($-0.086$, $-0.179$, $-0.007$; Table~\ref{tab:confirmDelta}).
G2, non-inferiority to the tuned ESN given the same kernel readout, passed only in
Stockholm. The losses are largest where the test inputs are most shifted (Lagos and
Mexico City, $+0.5$ training s.d.\ in temperature): the kernel extrapolates badly. The
kernel readout is withdrawn and the final design is unchanged. Scored descriptively,
the final design was non-inferior to the tuned ESN in Mexico City ($-0.0040$) and
Stockholm ($-0.0092$) and better than the tuned LSTM in all three cities, but in Lagos
it was clearly behind the ESN ($-0.0491$, CI $[-0.0649,-0.0360]$)---the largest gap in
any untouched city, and with Chennai (lower bound $-0.0220$) one of the two cities
outside the margin.

\paragraph*{Why Lagos.} (Post-hoc, descriptive; nine cities.) The Lagos gap grows with
horizon, from $+0.016$ ($T$, $h=1$) to $-0.159$ ($T$, $h=45$). Lagos temperature
anomalies (deviations from the seasonal cycle) are unusually persistent: their 30-day
autocorrelation is 0.32 (0.23 after removing the linear trend), against 0.02--0.12 in
the other eight cities, and across the nine cities this statistic is the strongest
correlate of the QRC$-$ESN gap ($r=-0.93$; driven by Lagos). Slow, small anomalies are
exactly what the QRC's shorter memory (Fig.~\ref{fig:memory}) cannot hold, so the Lagos
result locates the remaining gap rather than contradicting the others
(Fig.~\ref{fig:horizon}b).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figR3_horizon.png}
\caption{\label{fig:horizon}Test $R^2$ by forecast horizon on the nine untouched cities
(653-bin FID readout, $D=653$). (a) Mean over cities and the two variables for the final
QRC and the tuned baselines: the QRC matches the classical models at short horizons
and stays above the LSTM and linear AR, but the tuned ESN pulls ahead beyond about 10
days. (b) QRC minus tuned ESN per city; Lagos (blue) has the largest long-horizon gap.}

readout ($D=653$), regime A; ``final'' $=$ frozen gain $g=0.35$, ``standard'' $=g=1$.

\subsection{All nine untouched cities}
Pooling the descriptive comparisons over all nine confirmation cities
(Table~\ref{tab:pool9}, Fig.~\ref{fig:forest}) gives the summary we stand behind. The final design is close to
the tuned ESN but consistently below it (mean $\Delta=-0.0109$; ESN significantly
better in 6/9 cities, the QRC in none; within the 0.02 margin in 7/9, failing in
Chennai and Lagos). It is ahead of the tuned LSTM (mean $+0.0099$; 4/9 vs 2/9) and of
linear AR (mean $+0.0141$; 5/9 vs 0/9). The supported claim is \emph{non-inferiority}
of a physical QRC to tuned classical models on most untouched real-world forecasting
tasks, \emph{not} superiority to the tuned ESN.

\section{Pre-registered drift test}\label{sec:drift}
% Source: qrc_drift_{exchange,electricity}.json; QRC_Design_Concepts.md section 12 + "Drift test outcome".
The QRC's failure under input shift (ETTh1, ETTh2) was the clearest weakness of the
development benchmark, and step~5 suggested a remedy: re-centre each target on the
last observed value and append raw input lags (``level handling''). These are
classical features, not reservoir features; the same variant is given to the tuned
ESN. The drift test (commit \texttt{a4111de}, before the data were downloaded) applied
it to two untouched series (Sec.~\ref{sec:protocol}) with one primary criterion, D1:
level handling must beat the plain readout (CI excluding 0) on both. Bootstrap blocks
are 30 days (exchange) and 168 hours (electricity).

D1 passed on both series (Fig.~\ref{fig:drift}): $+0.058$ $[+0.013,+0.104]$ on the
exchange rate, whose test inputs lie $1.26$ training s.d.\ above the training mean, and
$+0.010$ $[+0.002,+0.016]$ on electricity, which barely shifts ($+0.02$ s.d.). The fix
works, but it brings no quantum edge. On the exchange rate the QRC with level handling
ties persistence (difference $-0.00004$, CI $[-0.0007,+0.0005]$) and edges past the
tuned ESN by $+0.001$: the series is close to a random walk, and level handling lets
the readout fall back to the last value. On electricity the QRC stays clearly behind
every tuned model (ESN $-0.074$, LSTM $-0.031$, linear AR $-0.034$).

\section{Mechanism on synthetic tasks (brief)}\label{sec:mechanism}
% Source: qrc_paired_tests.{json,md} (6-spin: 5 seeds learned vs arcsin incl. qrc_6spin_pub_shard{0,1}.json;
% 3 seeds vs tuned LSTM / ESN and tau->0); dccb7 J=0 ratios from qrc_dccb7_tau100{,_j0}.json;
% full mechanism tables and figures (figP1-figP4) are in QRC_Fair_Comparison.md, not in this paper.
Synthetic tasks are not the paper's performance claim; we use them only for ablations
that are too costly on multi-decade real series. They use the regime-B learned
per-spin encoding (Sec.~\ref{sec:regimes}), which needs gradients through the readout,
so they use the differentiable physics-informed line readout of
Sec.~\ref{sec:mech-readout} ($D=2D_{\mathrm{eff}}$, Table~\ref{tab:deff}).

On NARMA-2, NARMA-10~\cite{Atiya2000} and Mackey--Glass~\cite{MackeyGlass1977}
($h=10$), with a time-contiguous 50/25/25 split, the learned encoding beats the fixed
$\arcsin\sqrt{s}$ on every seed (Table~\ref{tab:synth}). Re-initializing the reservoir
before every step ($\tau\to0$) removes the gain, so it is carried by cross-step
reservoir memory; switching off all couplings ($J=0$) in the seven-spin dccb7 molecule
makes it ${\sim}38$--$126\times$ worse, so the spin--spin coupling carries most of the
computation. A tuned LSTM is beaten on NARMA-10 and Mackey--Glass, but a fully tuned
ESN (spectral radius, leak, input scale and penalty; also size-matched) is
${\sim}11$--$830\times$ better on every task. An ESN tuned over size alone had made
the QRC look competitive; tuning removed that impression, which is why the real-world
study tunes every baseline.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{\label{tab:synth}Synthetic tasks, abstract six-spin Ising reservoir,
reduced-FID readout ($D=322$): geometric-mean test-NMSE ratio of the learned encoding to
each comparator ($<1$ favours the learned QRC); in parentheses, seeds won by the
learned QRC / paired data seeds.}
\begin{ruledtabular}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
task & vs arcsin & vs $\tau\to0$ & vs tuned LSTM & vs tuned ESN \\ \colrule
NARMA-2      & 0.053 (5/5) & 0.0049 (3/3) & 1.42 (1/3) & 446 (0/3) \\
NARMA-10     & 0.41 (5/5)  & 0.12 (3/3)   & 0.49 (3/3) & 11.5 (0/3) \\
MG $h{=}10$  & 0.053 (5/5) & ---          & 0.58 (3/3) & 832 (0/3) \\
\end{tabular}
\end{ruledtabular}
\end{table}

On real data the learned encoding improved on arcsin at $g=1$ on 8 of 9 development
datasets (Table~\ref{tab:bench}), but the fixed gain $g=0.35$ captured that improvement
and learning on top of it added nothing (Sec.~\ref{sec:step4}). The real-world design
therefore keeps the physically simplest lever---how far each input pulse rotates the
stored state.

% ======================================================================
\section{Threats to validity}\label{sec:threats}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Simulation only.} All dynamics are simulated (exact Lindblad, measured
crotonic parameters). The simulation reads the FID from a copy of the state each step;
on hardware the readout disturbs the ensemble, so an experiment must re-run the input
history per readout point or use weak readout, at a real cost in experiment time.
\item \emph{One reservoir, one task family in confirmation.} The real-world results use a
single molecule (crotonic-9). All nine confirmation cities are ERA5 daily temperature
and humidity with one protocol; ERA5 is reanalysis, smoother than station data. Outside
daily weather the evidence is weaker: the development benchmark shows the QRC behind
(hourly data, Santa Fe) or failing (ETTh1/ETTh2), and on the untouched electricity
series it is behind every tuned model (Sec.~\ref{sec:drift}).
\item \emph{Margin chosen after Confirmation 1.} The non-inferiority margin $\delta=0.02$
was set knowing the Confirmation 1 CIs (Sec.~\ref{sec:confirm}); with a margin of $0.01$
Sydney would fail against the ESN (lower bound $-0.0128$), although F2-ESN would still
pass in 2/3 cities. The margin is
a judgement of practical equivalence, not a property of the data.
\item \emph{Seen development test sets.} The development benchmark's test blocks were
scored before the design work; although every design step used validation data only,
the concepts were motivated by those results. This is why every confirmation and the
drift test use data downloaded only after pre-registration. The Lagos explanation
(Sec.~\ref{sec:conf3}) is post-hoc and rests on nine cities.
\item \emph{Uncertainty model.} The bootstrap CIs resample test time for fixed fitted
models; they do not include replicate (seed) variance of the ESN and LSTM, which is
reported separately (Table~\ref{tab:bench}; replicate s.d.\ up to 0.0096 in the
confirmation cities). The
nine per-city comparisons per baseline are not corrected for multiplicity; we report
counts, not a pooled test.
\item \emph{Distribution shift.} Under input drift the QRC's nonlinear features
extrapolate badly; bounded transforms did not fix it, and a kernel readout made it
worse. Level handling fixes most of it (Sec.~\ref{sec:drift}), but it is a classical
addition to the readout, and only one of the two drift-test series is strongly shifted.
\item \emph{Mechanism study.} The ablations use the reduced-FID readout ($D=200$--$344$),
not the 653-bin standard, mostly on an abstract six-spin Ising model; comparisons with
the tuned classical models use three data seeds. They were not run on real-world data.
\item \emph{Six-qubit differentiability wall.} Regime B on the dense propagator is
limited to six qubits; the nine-spin and seven-spin campaigns use the block
propagator, and larger systems need checkpointing or parameter-shift gradients.
\end{enumerate}

% ======================================================================
\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
On real-world forecasting with chronological splits, validation-only development,
three pre-registered confirmations on nine untouched cities and a pre-registered drift
test, a simulated nine-spin NMR reservoir with the standard 653-bin FID readout is
non-inferior to a tuned ESN in 7/9 cities, to a tuned LSTM in 8/9 and to a tuned linear
AR model in 9/9, but never better than the tuned ESN, which is significantly ahead in
6/9. The step that made the QRC competitive was physical and simple: reducing the
encoding gain to $g=0.35$ to limit input overwrite. The remaining gap is long memory,
largest where slow anomalies dominate (Lagos). Five further pre-registered changes did
not help---including reading the long-lived $^{13}$C spins, which shows that the memory
gap is set by the write, not the readout. The QRC's failure under input shift is fixed
by classical level handling, which gives it no edge. We therefore report no quantum
advantage. The remaining lever is the write itself: storing inputs on spins that later
pulses do not touch (which, with a diagonal Hamiltonian, needs a coherent transfer
step), or longer-$T_1$, more strongly coupled molecules, followed by on-device tests.
